entries.caption:
The cheapest upgrade I ever made to my training was about 40 dollars, total, and none of it was a supplement.

I spent years treating sleep like the thing that happens after the real work. Then I started tracking it, and every bad session I could remember had a bad night attached to it. We spend almost a third of our life asleep and most guys treat it like dead time.

The stack I use and give to clients:

1. Mouth tape
Nose breathing all night instead of waking up dry at 4am. I switched to Sleepies because the old brand left residue on my face. Cheap, and you feel it by about the third night.

2. Magnetic nasal dilators
I've been on these a few weeks and I rate them above the mouth tape now. The adhesive strips fall off. These don't.

3. A real eye mask
Not the flimsy hotel one. Your bedroom is never as dark as you think it is.

4. No screens in the last 30 minutes
This one is free and it's the one everybody skips. Put the phone in another room, not face down next to you.

5. Same wake-up time, even after a bad night
Chasing sleep by sleeping in just moves the problem to tomorrow. Get up, get light, go again.

I call this an upgrade and not a habit for a reason. Every item is a one-time cost. You buy it once, you set it up once, and it keeps paying every night for years. Almost nothing else in training works like that.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic I use to find where someone is actually stuck.

Training six days a week was the most expensive habit I ever had, and for two years I called it discipline.

Nobody corrects you on this, because from the outside it looks like the right answer. More sessions, more commitment, more results. The bill shows up later, quietly, as numbers that stop moving.

What I changed:

1. Six days down to three
The first month felt like cheating. Then the lifts started moving again. Frequency was never the thing I was short on.

2. Rest days that are actually rest days
A rest day with 14,000 steps and a "light" session is a training day you're not counting. Rest or train, but be honest about which one you're doing.

3. Weight before volume
I stopped spamming reps and started loading the progressions. Load is the fastest road to the advanced skills. High volume builds endurance and then parks you.

4. Sleep tracked next to the lifts
Once both numbers sat on the same page it stopped being a mystery. The stalls had a pattern and the pattern was always upstream of the gym.

5. A deload the moment a lift stalls twice
Two bad sessions in a row is information, not a character flaw. Most people answer it with more work, which is exactly the wrong direction.

The thing nobody tells you is that overtraining doesn't feel like overtraining. It feels like discipline, right up until you look at three months of numbers and realise you paid for all of it and bought nothing.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

A client asked me last week which supplement would fix his testosterone. Honest answer: none of them, and the ones that promise to are selling you a way around four things you already know about.

I'm not a doctor, and if your bloodwork is genuinely off you need one. But most of the men who tell me their testosterone is low have a lifestyle problem wearing a medical costume.

The four that actually move it:

1. Sleep, 7 to 9 hours
Not 5 with caffeine stacked on top. Nine is a lot for most people, five isn't enough for anyone. This is the one that changes everything downstream of it.

2. Real food, simple and boring
Meat, fruit, vegetables. You don't need a protocol, you need to stop eating things that arrived in a wrapper. Colour on the plate beats any macro app.

3. Alcohol
I drank every weekend until I was 18, then lost Monday and part of Tuesday recovering from it. Two days a week, for years. Nobody counts the recovery days when they count the cost of a night out.

4. Nicotine
Cigarettes, vapes, pouches. I saw an enormous amount of vaping among 15 and 16 year olds when I lived in the UK, and it never registers as a health decision to the people doing it.

None of this costs money. That's exactly why it's a hard sell. A supplement lets you spend instead of change, and spending is easier.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

If a professional tells you to train a skill without loading it, remember something: he already owns the skill. He's describing the roof to someone who hasn't poured a foundation.

This is the most expensive piece of free advice in calisthenics and it costs beginners years.

What I actually give advanced clients:

1. Weighted progressions before the skill work
Dips, pull-ups, rows, all loaded. The strength has to exist before the shape of the movement means anything.

2. One skill at a time
Everything at once is the fastest way to go nowhere. One client came to me training every skill on the list and moving on none of them. Pick one, finish it, move.

3. Load added in small blocks, not jumps
The jump feels productive and buys you a wrist problem. Small blocks are boring and they keep you training.

4. Volume as a finisher, not as the plan
Reps build endurance. Endurance is not what's stopping you from holding a lean planche.

5. Film it, or you're guessing
You will feel a position you're not in. Everyone does, including me. The camera settles the argument in four seconds.

What you see online is guys floating with nothing on them. Every one of them built it under load first. That part doesn't get filmed because it isn't worth watching.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

A client told me he had no time for a routine. So I stopped giving him a routine and gave him five things instead, none of which take a real block out of his day.

I hear "no time" on almost every call. Most of the people saying it genuinely are buried, so I've stopped arguing with the sentence. I just don't build the plan around it anymore.

The five:

1. Real food, three or four times a day
Not a diet. Food you cooked, with more than one colour on the plate. Cook more, buy less.

2. Get outside and move
Walk, get sun, exist outdoors for a while. It doesn't have to be training and it shouldn't be. It's also the only hour of my day where I actually think about my own decisions.

3. Water where you can see it
Put the bottle in your line of sight. Once it's visible it becomes almost impossible to ignore. Sounds too simple to matter. It's the one clients report back on most.

4. Track the streak
An app, a journal, doesn't matter. Motivation is downstream of watching a number go up, not the other way around.

5. One hour on Sunday where you eat what you want
No guilt, and don't call it a cheat. Skip this one and you'll quit in seven weeks feeling like a robot who failed.

We're not going for perfect. We're going for efficient and repeatable. One percent, and then again tomorrow.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

I stopped relying on willpower the day I started moving objects around my apartment. Sounds like a joke. It's the highest-return change I've made to how I coach.

I'll tell a client something on a call, he'll agree with it completely, and he'll have forgotten it by Tuesday. That's not a discipline problem. It's a design problem, and you fix a design problem with objects, not effort.

What I set up, and what I give clients:

1. The water bottle in your line of sight
Not in the kitchen. Where you sit. Once you see it, drinking it stops being a decision.

2. Keys and phone across the room from the bar
One client kept losing a cue between calls. Now the thing he has to pick up anyway sits next to the thing he keeps forgetting.

3. Clothes out the night before
The session doesn't start at the gym. It starts at the point where you'd have to make a decision, and this removes one.

4. Phone charging in another room
Not face down on the nightstand. Another room. Face down is a negotiation and you will lose it at 6am.

5. One object per habit, no more
Five cues at once is decoration, and your eye stops seeing decoration in about four days.

Almost none of this is about the object. It's that you decided in advance, while you were calm, instead of at 6am when you're not. That's the whole trick.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

A client of mine trades for a living. He understood risk perfectly at work and was running his training like the worst portfolio you've ever seen.

Everything on one position. All the sessions, all the attention, all the emotional weight on one skill he wanted this month. And when it didn't move, the whole thing was down.

So we talked about it in his language:

1. You have a portfolio of skills
Push, pull, legs, core, one skill goal. You're a broker. You're not putting every chip in the same place.

2. Concentration gets you hurt faster
Not just frustrated. Same joint, same angle, every session, is how you buy an elbow problem you'll pay off for three months.

3. Concentration gets you frustrated faster too
One position, one source of feedback. When it stalls, and it will stall, nothing else is reporting a gain and you quit.

4. Diversifying doesn't mean doing everything
Everything at once is the opposite error and it's just as bad. Three or four positions, weighted differently. Not eleven.

5. Rebalance every couple of weeks, not every session
Two-week blocks. One week of high-intensity combos that double as active recovery, one week of standard progressions to break PRs. You don't check a portfolio hourly and you shouldn't check your training that way either.

He got it in about ninety seconds, because he already knew all of it. He'd just never applied it to himself.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

I wish more men knew that eating properly is cheaper than eating badly. Not spiritually cheaper. Cheaper on the receipt.

The expensive version is the one that arrives ready. Delivery, the meal deal, the protein bar that costs three euros and does the job of an egg. People run the numbers on a gym membership and never once run them on the way they're currently eating.

What I give every client:

1. Cook more, buy less
That's the entire guide in four words. Everything below is a footnote to it.

2. Three or four real meals, no snacking
Snacks don't make much physiological sense for most people and they're where the day quietly falls apart. Eat properly, then stop eating.

3. Protein at 1.6 to 1.8 grams per kilo if you're building
That's the number. You don't need to weigh food for the rest of your life, you need to know roughly where you land.

4. Colour on the plate
Better shortcut than any tracking app, because you can check it with your eyes in one second.

5. The 80/20 rule, and mean it
Eighty percent real food, the rest is your life. I've eaten that way for years and it works precisely because it doesn't ask you to be a different person on weekends.

I ask clients not to obsess about eating one hundred percent clean. Obsession has a failure rate near a hundred percent, and it's the reason most people are on their fifth restart.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

When a client's numbers stall, more training is the last thing I add. Usually it's the first thing he already tried, alone, for six weeks, before telling me.

A plateau is almost never a work problem. It's a recovery problem with a work problem's symptoms, and from inside the gym those look identical.

What I check, in this order:

1. Sleep, before anything else
Not how many hours he thinks he got. What he actually tracked. This resolves it more often than everything else on the list combined.

2. How many days he's really training
Including the "light" ones, including the run he doesn't count. The real number is almost always higher than the number he tells me.

3. Whether a PR happened recently
A front lever dipping right after a PR week isn't a regression, it's the bill. Normal, and it clears with active recovery, not more volume.

4. What's happening outside the gym
Shifts, a move, a bad month at work. The body doesn't keep a separate budget for stress from your job.

5. Only then, the program
And usually the fix is less frequency with more intensity, which is the opposite of what he was about to do.

Adding volume to a stalled lift is the most expensive move in training. You pay in weeks, you get nothing back, and you finish with less than you started with.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

I track how my clients fail, not just what they lift. Sounds like a consolation prize. It's the most useful number I have.

When someone sends me a failed rep, the first thing I ask isn't what went wrong. It's whether he failed better or worse than last time. Almost nobody has an answer, because nobody is measuring the thing that's actually moving.

What I look at:

1. Where in the range it broke down
Failing at 45 degrees when you used to fail at 70 is progress with a failed rep attached. That's a win and it should be logged as one.

2. Whether the form held until the failure
Clean until it stopped is a completely different result from ugly the whole way. One means add load. The other means go back a step.

3. How fast the first reps moved
The rep that counts is often the one before the one you're watching. If rep one was slow, rep four was never happening.

4. What the second attempt looked like
Everybody has a bad first set. The second one tells you whether it was the body or the day.

5. How he described it before I said anything
I ask "how did that feel?" before I correct. If he already knows, my job that week is much smaller.

Track only what you complete and you get feedback maybe once a month. Track how you fail and you get it every session. That's the difference between people who move and people who repeat the same year.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

I did this so you don't have to. I stopped buying pre-workout and replaced it with about sixty cents of food.

I'm not against caffeine and I won't pretend the powder does nothing. The problem is what it hides. It's very good at getting a tired person into the gym, which means you never find out why you were tired.

What I use instead, and what I give clients:

1. Dates, honey, water with a bit of salt
That's the whole thing. Fast carbs and electrolytes, about thirty minutes out. Costs nothing and doesn't leave you wired at 11pm.

2. Coffee, but not on an empty stomach
And not at 6pm, whatever your tolerance is telling you. Caffeine has a half-life whether or not you feel it.

3. Actually eating before the session
Half the people who need pre-workout need lunch. They've just never tested the difference.

4. Train at the hour you have energy, not the hour you decided
One of my clients trains after a full day of work and business travel. We built the plan around when he could genuinely push, not around a schedule that looked good on paper.

5. If you need it every single session, that's the signal
Needing a stimulant to start every workout isn't a preference. It's a sleep problem sending you a bill.

None of this is anti-supplement. I take creatine and omega-3 and I've said so plenty of times. It's that pre-workout is the one people buy to avoid answering a question, and the question is free.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

A client showed me his supplement shelf on a call. Somewhere around two hundred dollars sitting there. Three of them were doing something and the rest was a subscription to feeling like he was making progress.

I'm not anti-supplement. I'm against buying them in the order most people buy them, which is exciting first and useful last.

The short list:

1. Creatine, 5 grams a day
Most researched thing on the shelf, cheapest thing on the shelf, and it doesn't matter when you take it. If you buy one item, this is it.

2. Protein powder, only if you're actually short
It's food, not a supplement. If you're already hitting 1.6 to 1.8 grams per kilo with real meals you don't need it and you're paying more per gram for the privilege.

3. Omega 3
Boring, well-supported, and almost nobody gets enough of it from what they eat.

4. Bloodwork before anything else
Vitamins and minerals are worth taking once you know what you're low on. Before that you're guessing expensively.

5. Be suspicious of a low price
If a product is much cheaper than everything near it, or won't tell you exactly what's inside, there's a reason and you're the one absorbing it.

Here's the part that matters. Every item on this list is a rounding error next to sleep, food and showing up. Supplements are the last five percent, and almost everyone shopping for them is trying to buy their way out of the other ninety-five.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

I once gave a client a 90 pound dip knowing he'd get one rep at most. I told him afterwards that I'd done it on purpose, because I wanted to see if he was ready for the big leagues.

That isn't cruelty and it isn't a motivation trick. Deliberate overload is a tool, and it's the fastest way I know to move something that isn't in the muscle.

How I use it:

1. Only once the base is real
This is not for someone still building the foundation. Load something that isn't ready and you get an injury, not a lesson.

2. The failure has to be safe
Set it up so the worst outcome is racking it and walking away. If failing is dangerous, it isn't a tool, it's a gamble.

3. Say beforehand that failing is fine
"If you hit 45 degrees and can't push, it's still a win." Without that sentence the whole thing costs him confidence instead of building it.

4. Once, not weekly
It works because it's rare. Program it every week and it stops being a signal and becomes bad programming.

5. Then straight back to the boring progression
The heavy single tells him what his body can hold. The boring blocks are what make it his.

What changes isn't strength, it's the ceiling in his head. He stops treating the next number as a wall. The body was ready before he was, which is true far more often than people think.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

The valuable part of this isn't the plan. It's that on Tuesday somebody is going to ask.

I used to think I was selling programs. Then I watched which clients stayed and what they actually used, and it wasn't the routines. Exercises are free and have been for a decade.

What a week actually looks like:

1. Life first, not the body
Work, sleep, travel, family. If I don't know what his week was, I'm giving advice to a spreadsheet.

2. The videos, with the reason attached
I watch what he filmed and I correct with the why. Not "elbows at 45." Elbows at 45, and here's what your shoulder does at 90.

3. The question before the correction
"How did that feel?" and "did you fail better or worse than last time?" first. A correction he arrived at himself survives the week. Mine doesn't always.

4. The plan bent to his real life
Twelve hour shifts means a week with no new exercises. Harvest season means short sessions at home. The plan adapts or it gets abandoned. Those are the only two options.

5. Three things, said out loud at the end
Never more than three. Then I tell him I'm going to message him about them anyway, so he feels like he owes someone an answer.

One client told me straight out that he needed other people to expect something from him. Not motivation. Expectation. Most disciplined people aren't self-powered, they're just honest about what actually moves them.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

My richest client never asked what something cost.

He asked what it would cost him to keep doing it the way he was already doing it.

I trained him in person for almost three years, 45 minutes on the bike each way. That question is the most useful thing anyone ever taught me about training, and he wasn't talking about training.

Here's what I changed after it:

1. I stopped counting money and started counting years
Two years of half effort is more expensive than any coach. You get the money back. You don't get the two years back.

2. I stopped selling cheap plans
I ran that model for a while. Cheap plan, no accountability, people quit in week three and blamed themselves. Nobody won.

3. Every client needs a date, a test or a person
Not "get in shape". The ones who stay for months always have one. A fire department application, a deployment, a birthday they picked.

4. I raised my prices and the results got better
He told me to charge him more. He said he was paying for the outcome, not the hour. He was right.

5. I ask the same question on every call now
What is this already costing you. Most guys have never done that math out loud, and it changes the whole conversation.

The expensive part was never the coaching. It was the three years before it.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free guide.

A client added up what quitting kept costing him.

Memberships he paid through, two programs, a bike he used four times, and eleven months of starting again every January. It came out to more than a year of coaching.

He wasn't broke. He was paying in instalments for something he never finished.

Here's what we changed:

1. We cut the plan in half
He was trying to train six days. Six days is what you do when you're negotiating with guilt, not building a body. We went to three.

2. We killed the restart
Restarting is harder than starting. A client told me that once and she was right. So we built a week that survives a bad week instead of one that needs a perfect one.

3. We tracked one thing
A streak. Not macros, not steps, not sleep score. One box to tick. Motivation dies, a streak you don't want to break doesn't.

4. Sunday stays free
One meal, no logging, no guilt. The people who last aren't the most disciplined ones, they're the ones who never feel like they're in jail.

5. He stopped buying and started finishing
No new app, no new supplement, no new split. He finished the boring one.

The money was never the problem. The eleven Januaries were.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free guide.

Going fast costs you the next ten years. Going far only costs you this one.

I used to think all in was the only setting. Train five or six days, cut hard, sleep whenever. It works for about eleven weeks and then it takes the following year off you.

Here's what going far actually looks like:

1. Three training days, not six
Fewer sessions, heavier work, real recovery. Most guys aren't undertrained. They're under-recovered and calling it discipline.

2. One or two runs a week
Not a marathon block. Just enough that the engine keeps up with the body.

3. Whole food, 80/20
No versus food, no banned list. Eighty percent real, twenty percent whatever your life actually looks like.

4. One skill at a time
A client came to me doing everything and going nowhere. We picked one movement and left the rest alone for six weeks. He felt his back for the first time in years.

5. A bad week is part of the plan
Not something to recover from. Your standard is higher now, so your worst week today beats your best week two years ago. You just stopped noticing.

Fast is a decision. Far is a system.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free guide.

A client told me he feels guilty resting. That guilt is the most expensive habit he owns.

He trains through it. Then he trains through the fatigue the guilt created. Then he wonders why nothing has moved since March.

Here's what we did about it:

1. Rest days went into the program in writing
Not "if you need it". Scheduled, same as a session. If it isn't written down it's a negotiation, and guilt wins every negotiation.

2. A flat lift is a recovery problem first
Losing your front lever the week after a PR is normal. It isn't a signal to add volume. Almost every plateau I've seen was overtraining in a discipline costume.

3. Sleep got treated like training
Mouth tape, nasal dilators, dark room, no screens for the last half hour. We spend most of our life asleep and nobody takes it seriously.

4. Active recovery replaced doing nothing
Low intensity combos, a walk, some sun. He needed permission to move without it counting as a session.

5. We tracked how he failed, not only what he lifted
Failing better is progress. Once he could see that, resting stopped feeling like quitting.

Guilt isn't discipline. It's the tax you pay for not trusting your own plan.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free guide.

A client with four jobs stopped budgeting his time. He started budgeting his energy instead.

Marine, four jobs, studying for a test on the side. He told me he had no time. He had the same twenty-four hours as everyone else. What he didn't have was a plan for which of them were worth anything.

Here's what changed:

1. We stopped asking when and started asking what's left
A session after an eighteen hour day isn't a session. The hard work moved to the two windows where he still had something in the tank.

2. Three real sessions beat six half ones
He was aiming for six and hitting two, and feeling behind on both counts. Three planned, three done, no debt.

3. Shifts and travel got their own version of the week
Short sessions at home, nothing new to learn. The plan bends to the life. The life doesn't bend to the plan.

4. Visual hooks instead of willpower
Keys next to the dumbbells. Bottle on the desk. You'll forget what I told you on the call. You won't forget the thing sitting in your way.

5. Sleep became the first lever instead of the last
He wasn't unmotivated. He was cooked. Mindset was never his problem.

Everybody gets twenty-four hours. The question is which four you're protecting.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free guide.

He spent 400 dollars a year on supplements to fix what sleep fixes for free.

Zinc, magnesium, three testosterone boosters, and a pre workout he needed just to get through the session. Low energy, flat lifts, nothing in the morning. He wanted to know which one to add next.

None of them. Here's the order that actually works:

1. Sleep
Seven to nine hours. Nine is a lot, five isn't enough. This is the whole thing, and it's the one nobody wants to hear because you can't buy it.

2. Real food
Meat, fruit, vegetables, three or four colorful plates a day. Cooking more and buying less will do more for your energy than anything with a label on it.

3. Alcohol
I stopped at eighteen. I used to lose Monday and Tuesday to a Saturday. If you drink every weekend you're not training four days a week, you're training two and recovering two.

4. Nicotine
Vapes included. Especially vapes.

5. Then, maybe, supplements
Creatine, omega 3, bloodwork before any of it. They're the last five percent. He was trying to buy the first ninety five.

The supplements weren't the expensive part. Using them to avoid the free stuff was.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free guide.

Nobody in that gym is coming over to fix your elbows.

That's the real reason you've been at the same number for a year. Not discipline, not genetics, not the program you downloaded at 2am. You've just never had anyone watch you do it.

You can be consistent for years in the wrong position. Consistency protects you from quitting. It doesn't protect you from being wrong.

Comment PULL UP and I'll send you the free guide.

Your biceps are not supposed to be the sore part.

If your arms are cooked the day after and your back feels like nothing happened, that wasn't a bad session. It was a good session for a muscle you weren't aiming at.

That's why the number never moves. You keep asking the smallest link in the chain to do the job of the biggest one, and then you call yourself weak when it taps out at rep eight.

You were never weak. You were just pulling with the wrong thing.

Comment PULL UP and I'll send you the free guide.

Everybody has tried a pull up with 20 kilos once. Almost nobody has done eight sets with five.

The first one is a video. The second one is what actually moves your number, and nobody films it because there's nothing to film. It looks like a guy with a small plate doing sets that don't even look hard.

What you see online is people flying on a bar with nothing hanging off them. They all did the boring weighted version first, for years, off camera. You're copying the end of someone's process and wondering why it doesn't do anything for you.

Light enough to hold the position. Heavy enough that it isn't free. That's the whole thing.

Comment PULL UP and I'll send you the free guide.

Your back didn't fail on that set. Your hands did.

Sweaty palms on a steel bar and suddenly half your effort goes into not sliding off it. Then you count that as a back exercise.

It costs less than your protein shake. Chalk. That's the whole fix, and it sounds too small to matter until you do a set without it.

Most of what's holding your pull ups is that size. Not a new program, not two more days a week. Small things nobody bothered to tell you, sitting there for years, quietly costing you reps.

Comment PULL UP and I'll send you the free guide.

Doing it more times doesn't fix doing it wrong.

Most guys answer a stuck number with more volume. More sets, more days, more of the same rep that was already going to the wrong muscle. Three months later the number hasn't moved and now the elbows hurt too.

I did exactly that for a long time. Training alone in a park, no idea what I was doing, and when it rained I couldn't train at all. I still thought my problem was frequency.

A bad position repeated a thousand times is just a thousand bad positions. It doesn't average out into a good one.

Fix where you're pulling from. Then earn the volume.

Comment PULL UP and I'll send you the free guide.

You can do the same exercise for two years and never actually do it once.

I trained alone in a park for two years before anyone told me anything. No coach, no camera, no idea what my back was supposed to feel like. I just added reps and hoped.

A client of mine did calisthenics for years and only ever felt his forearms and his biceps. We changed how he held the bar and he messaged me after that session saying he felt his back for the first time in his life. Same exercise. Same guy. Same bar.

Nobody is going to walk over in the gym and fix your elbows. That's the part people never budget for. They budget for the membership, the program, the protein. Never for someone watching them do it.

Your pull ups aren't stuck because you're weak. They're stuck because nothing is telling you where the load is going.

Comment PULL UP and I'll send you the free guide.

They sell you sleep in a bottle.

Zinc, magnesium, three testosterone boosters, and a pre workout you need just to get through the session. A client of mine was spending four hundred dollars a year on that shelf and wanted to know which one to add next.

None of them. He was sleeping five hours.

Seven to nine hours. Nine is a lot, five isn't enough for anyone. It's the whole thing, and it's the one nobody wants to hear because you can't buy it. The supplements weren't the expensive part. Using them to avoid the free part was.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

You don't want the body. You want to have wanted it.

There's a version of this where you're already three years in and it's just Tuesday and you train. That's the one people actually want. Not the work, the state of having done the work.

The gap between those two is about eleven weeks of nothing visible happening. Week one you're excited. Week three nothing has changed yet and the only thing holding it together is that you said you would.

Almost everyone quits in that gap, then decides the problem was the program.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

Most online coaches have never kept a client past month three.

Month one is easy, everything is new. Month two the novelty is gone. Month three is where a coach either has something or doesn't, because by then the plan isn't the product any more. The follow-up is.

I've had clients run four, six, seven check-ins straight. What kept them wasn't the program. It was that someone was going to ask.

One told me straight out that he needed other people to expect something from him. Not motivation. Expectation. Most disciplined people aren't self-powered, they're just honest about what actually moves them.

Comment MENTALITY and I'll send you the free diagnostic.

You're not undertrained. You're under-recovered and calling it discipline.
